## Two names, one key

Ask Sonic Pi for `note(:fs4)` and for `note(:gb4)` and both hand back 66. Same
key, same frequency, same sound. So why does written music keep both names
around?

Because they describe different motion. F-sharp is an F pushed up toward G.
G-flat is a G pulled down toward F. That's *enharmonic spelling*: two names for
one sounding pitch in equal temperament. While your program only plays isolated
notes, the distinction looks like clutter. It stops looking like clutter the
moment you name an interval, explain where a melody is heading, or export
notation.

The table below carries both layers at once. `:pitch` is the number that makes
sound. `:spelling` is the label that keeps your intention visible in the log.

## Print the label, play the number

```{.ruby audio=""}
use_bpm 80
use_synth :piano

spellings = [
  {pitch: note(:fs4), spelling: "F-sharp"},
  {pitch: note(:gb4), spelling: "G-flat"},
  {pitch: note(:as4), spelling: "A-sharp"},
  {pitch: note(:bb4), spelling: "B-flat"}
]

spellings.each do |entry|
  puts "#{entry[:spelling]} -> #{entry[:pitch]}"
  play entry[:pitch], release: 0.6
  sleep 1
end
```

Each pair gives you the same keyboard pitch twice. No waveform says "sharp" on
the first attack and "flat" on the second. Meanwhile the log holds two
different labels against two identical integers. That redundancy is the point:
the fields answer different questions.

## Add the pairs yourself

1. Add C-sharp4 and D-flat4. Both map to 61 and sound the same. Keep the labels
   printing so the numeric equality doesn't quietly erase them.

2. Restore the table and print integers only. Playback still works perfectly.
   Now name one later task that the stripped output can no longer support.

3. Restore the labels and add B-sharp4 alongside C5. Read the values Sonic Pi
   returns and watch the spelling walk across an octave boundary. Letter name
   and octave number can't be read independently of each other.

## Why the label outlives the collapse

Spelling is metadata on a numeric pitch, and metadata here isn't decoration.
The integer decides what you hear. The label carries the note's role into
analysis, explanation and notation. You've kept a source identifier beside a
normalised key before; two rows matching on the key never meant you could throw
the source away.

No single spelling wins everywhere. Key, chord and melodic direction between
them make F-sharp the informative name in one bar and G-flat the informative
name in the next. Normalising every class to a global sharp name tidies your
transposition arithmetic and deletes the evidence a correct musical explanation
needs.

Interval naming shows the cost in one line. C-sharp to E spans the letters
C-D-E, so it's some kind of third. D-flat to E spans D-E, so it's some kind of
second. Both cover three semitones. Subtracting MIDI numbers reports the
distance and can't recover the letter span, which is why [Lesson 18](../04-intervals/18-interval-carries-two-measurements.qmd) measures
both.

Until then, read the two views together. Identical sounds confirm the shared
address; distinct labels preserve what the address collapsed. [Lesson 11](11-pentatonic-scale-with-no-wrong-notes.qmd) dodges
the whole question for a while by asking Sonic Pi for a ready-made five-note
collection and treating its members as plain numbers.

## A table for all twelve

Build a spelling table covering all twelve classes. Where a class carries both
a sharp and a flat name in common use, store two hashes for it. Give each hash
a `:pitch` and a `:spelling`, and print both before the note plays.

Check that twelve distinct numeric classes appear and that every label you
supplied is still there. Then audition it in Sonic Pi 5. Enharmonic partners
land on one sound and one integer while their printed names stay apart. See
both facts at once and your data model is carrying playback and intent
together.
